questions.q: What is the article mainly about?
options: How families can reduce their risk of catching seasonal flu viruses
Why athletes in their prime sometimes die of sudden heart attacks
How biomarkers are found, including cell villages for vulnerability markers
How the FDA came to approve the first A1c-based diabetes diagnostic
questions.explain: It explains biomarkers and the author's cell village method for finding genetic biomarkers.

questions.q: In which decade did scientists first see unusually high protein levels in diabetics' blood, leading to the A1c test?
questions.explain: The A1c test's origins date to the 1960s; the FDA approved it in 2013.

options: A network of clinics that share patient blood test data
A public database of genetic variants linked to disease
Stem cell-derived cells from many people pooled in one dish
A lab facility for growing bacteria under controlled conditions
questions.explain: The author pools brain cells from dozens to hundreds of people in one dish and uses their genomes as barcodes.

questions.q: What range of Zika infection did they see across 40 people's cells?
options: Between 20% and 80%
Under 1% to over 99%
Always about 50%
Between 10% and 50%
questions.explain: For some fewer than 1% of cells were infected, for others more than 99%.

questions.q: What is the author's likely view of traditional cell studies with few donors?
options: They are unnecessary since GWAS suffices
They are more reliable than cell villages
They are cheaper and therefore better
They can't capture natural human diversity
questions.explain: Small donor numbers cannot capture diversity or explain why an exposure sickens one person but not another.
